## Abstract

Visual perception serves as the primary sensory modality for autonomous robots navigating and interacting with complex environments. However, robotic vision systems frequently encounter challenging illumination conditions—such as low-light indoor corridors, high-contrast outdoor scenes, and backlit industrial workspaces—that severely degrade the quality of captured images, directly compromising downstream robotic tasks including object detection, semantic segmentation, and visual SLAM. Deep learning-based methods have achieved remarkable success in image enhancement, but traditional approaches often necessitate paired datasets for training, incurring high costs for acquiring paired pre- and post-optimized images in real-world robotic scenarios. This paper introduces a lightweight image enhancement network named Cycle Bilateral Generative Adversarial Networks (CBGAN), specifically designed for real-time visual perception in robotic systems. Based on an unsupervised cyclic generative adversarial network architecture, CBGAN optimizes images by learning to predict both local and global affine transformations within the bilateral space in a low-resolution stream, and subsequently applying these transformations to the full-resolution domain. Specifically, CBGAN employs adversarial training, incorporating inverse mapping and cycle consistency loss, to ensure high-quality enhancement within an unsupervised training paradigm. In unsupervised scenarios, CBGAN outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Our network processes a 4 K image in tens of milliseconds. Compared with the conventional CycleGAN employing ResNet generators, our method achieves an approximate 95.8% reduction in parameter count and operates over 170 times faster, demonstrating immense potential for real-time deployment on resource-constrained robotic platforms.

## ABSTRACT

Real-world low-light images face multiple challenges. Non-uniform illumination, under-exposed regions and severe texture degradation are common. These factors make reliable enhancement difficult to achieve. Many existing unsupervised methods rely on simplified illumination assumptions. Others use coarse pixel-level constraints. Under spatially varying illumination, these approaches often lead to over-enhancement. They can also cause a loss of structural details. This paper introduces DAF-Net (dual-path adaptive frequency network). It is a lightweight unsupervised framework for low-light enhancement. The framework explicitly models multi-attention feature refinement. It also decouples the estimation of enhancement parameters and intensity. The network processes features through a sequence of attention modules. These include illumination-aware attention, adaptive frequency attention, dual-path context attention and dynamic recovery attention. This design effectively extracts under-exposed regions, frequency-sensitive features, contextual dependencies and spatial details. The framework estimates enhancement parameters and spatially varying intensity maps separately. These two branches are jointly optimized. This provides fine-grained control over colour adjustment and enhancement strength. Three refined unsupervised loss terms work together. They regulate texture preservation, illumination smoothness and exposure distribution. A perceptual consistency loss serves as an auxiliary constraint. It helps maintain the semantic coherence of the enhanced image. Experiments are conducted on LSRW, MIT-Adobe FiveK and LOL-v2-real datasets. Results show that DAF-Net delivers stable and competitive performance. It achieves average LPIPS, PSNR and SSIM values of 0.169, 19.591 and 0.707, respectively.

Self-calibrated methods exploit internal image statistics for enhancement. Self-calibrated illumination (SCI) [28] assumes that properly exposed regions exist within an image and uses them as references to guide illumination adjustment in darker areas. Pyramid-based and lightweight designs further extend unsupervised enhancement to more efficient architectures. Progressive self-enhancement network (PSENet) [29] employs pyramid semantic embeddings with attention mechanisms to capture multi-scale contextual cues, while lightweight unsupervised curve estimation network (LEES-Net) [30] and LEES-Net+ emphasize computational efficiency for practical deployment. Although unsupervised methods reduce data dependency, they face intrinsic trade-offs between quantitative accuracy and perceptual quality. Many approaches lack explicit noise modelling, implicitly amplifying noise along with signal during enhancement. As a result, achieving stable illumination correction, texture preservation and perceptual consistency within a unified unsupervised framework remains an open challenge. We also note recent works such as neural implicit Fourier transform (NeFour) [31] and cross-modal spherical aggregation network (S2-ShadowNet) [32], which address low-illumination or shadow removal in different domains. While these methods are not specifically designed for low-light image enhancement, they highlight the broader interest in handling illumination-degraded imagery. Accordingly, we do not perform direct performance comparisons with these methods, as their objectives and application domains differ from the low-light image enhancement task considered in this work.

### 3.2 Baseline Enhancement Formulation

Unsupervised low-light image enhancement is commonly addressed by learning a direct enhancement mapping from the input image, without requiring paired normal-light supervision. Among existing approaches, the DCE [14] paradigm formulates enhancement as an iterative pixel-wise adjustment process, which has demonstrated effectiveness and stability under unsupervised settings. DAF-Net adopts this enhancement-by-mapping principle as the baseline formulation, while extending it to achieve improved adaptivity and robustness.

Let $$I \in [0,1]^{H \times W \times 3}$$ denote a low-light input image. Instead of reconstructing a target image, the enhancement process is formulated as a transformation applied directly to the input:

$$$$\begin{equation} I_{\text{enh}} = \mathcal {F}(I), \end{equation}$$$$(4)

where $$\mathcal {F}(\cdot)$$ represents a learnable enhancement function. This formulation avoids explicit reliance on reference images and allows the network to be trained in a fully unsupervised manner.
## 5 Conclusion

This paper addresses the problem of unsupervised low-light image enhancement under complex and non-uniform illumination conditions and proposes DAF-Net, a lightweight enhancement framework based on residual enhancement modeling. By decoupling enhancement direction and intensity, the proposed method achieves stable illumination correction while reducing over-enhancement and colour distortion. The multi-attention design captures illumination variations and spatial context, enabling accurate enhancement of under-exposed regions while preserving well-lit areas. In addition, the unsupervised loss design introduces complementary constraints on illumination smoothness, texture preservation and exposure control, which jointly improve perceptual quality and structural fidelity. Experimental evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that DAF-Net achieves competitive performance with a compact model size, confirming its effectiveness and practicality for real-world low-light image enhancement. Although DAF-Net achieves competitive performance in unsupervised low-light image enhancement, several limitations remain. First, in extremely low-light regions with severe sensor noise, the enhancement process may amplify noise patterns because the current framework does not explicitly model noise. Second, minor colour artefacts may appear in some regions under complex illumination conditions, where the estimated enhancement parameters are not perfectly accurate. Future work will focus on addressing these aspects.

## Abstract

This paper presents a lightweight, unsupervised image enhancement method based on existing models, termed LCCDnet (Light-curve and Color-decoupled). The method separates the enhancement task into light enhancement and detail optimization. Images are decomposed into HSV channels: HS channels manage image details, while the V channel controls brightness. A light curve is applied to estimate brightness enhancement, with design considerations for pixel value range, monotonicity, and differentiability. For HS channels, a method inspired by the Purkinje effect decomposes the channel into two intrinsic color values, which are then combined into a novel HS channel. LCCDnet does not require paired or unpaired data for training. The method achieves image enhancement through intuitive nonlinear curve mapping, focusing on image details. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Abstract

Most existing low-light image enhancement (LIE) methods rely on expensive paired low-light and normal-light datasets, while unsupervised approaches depend on handcrafted priors to design networks or select similar normal-light images as pseudo-references, limiting their generalization and robustness. To address these challenges, we propose a novel differentiable histogram-guided unsupervised Retinex enhancement (DHURE) method, which leverages the distribution of illumination histograms in real-world scenarios to achieve high-fidelity color preservation and refined brightness distribution across diverse extremely low-light images. DHURE avoids reliance on scene-specific features and effectively captures both fine-grained details and overall brightness information. Specifically, our method consists of two key components: 1) The lightweight architecture of DHURE is composed of Retinex decomposition and illumination enhancement. We perform Retinex decomposition on paired low-light images (PRD) and design the Illumination Histogram-guided Enhancement (IHE) module. Both modules employ lightweight architectures. 2) To fully exploit the adaptive priors inherent in paired low-light images, we introduce a self-supervised reflectance map loss that aligns with the Retinex basis loss. Based on the illumination distribution of real-world normal-light images, we define two unsupervised illumination histogram losses, enabling more generalized and robust enhancement. Extensive and diverse experiments demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance compared to existing unsupervised LIE approaches, showing superior results on most evaluation metrics. The source code is available at https://github.com/yoonyin/DHURE-main.

##### Summary

Infrared images captured in complex scenes often have low contrast and weakened fine structures, which can degrade visual interpretation and downstream performance. We present UIRENet, a lightweight unsupervised network for infrared image enhancement based on an image-adaptive target-gradient prior. For each input, we construct a target gradient map using noise-suppressed gradients and clipped adaptive gradient histogram equalization, then train the network without paired data with a gradient-map registration loss and total variation regularization. The enhanced image is produced via iterative pixel-wise curve adjustment. UIRENet has 0.082M parameters and requires 36.6 GFLOPs for a 512 × 512 input, with 0.99 ms inference on an RTX 4090. We further extend the efficiency analysis with GPU and CPU latency measurements.

Existing deep learning methods often rely on large networks and labeled datasets, limiting their deployment on resource-constrained platforms. In this paper, we propose LiteIE, an ultra-lightweight unsupervised enhancement framework that eliminates dependence on large-scale supervision and generalizes well across diverse conditions. We design a backbone-agnostic feature extractor with only two convolutional layers to produce compact image features enhancement tensors. In addition, we develop a parameter-free Iterative Restoration Module, which reuses the extracted features to progressively recover fine details lost in earlier enhancement steps, without introducing any additional learnable parameters. We further propose an unsupervised training objective that integrates exposure control, edge-aware smoothness, and multi-scale color consistency losses. Experiments on the LOL dataset, LiteIE achieves 19.04 dB PSNR, surpassing SOTA by 1.4 dB while using only 0.07\% of its parameters.
